text: To train a network we will need to know, for every single weight, how a small change to it would change the final error. Before we can answer that, we need a precise record of how the output was computed in the first place, and the cleanest such record is a picture called a computational graph.

Take a small expression: multiply a by b, add c, and multiply the result by f. A computational graph breaks it into elementary operations. Each operation is a node, each number travels along an edge, and the edges show which results feed into which operations. It is like the flowchart of a recipe, where every step names the ingredients it uses and hands its product on to the next step.

Running the forward pass means pushing actual numbers through the graph from left to right. With a equal to two and b equal to minus three, the first node produces minus six. Adding c, which is ten, gives four, and multiplying by f, which is minus two, gives a final output of minus eight. Every node computes its value only after all of its inputs are ready, so the order of evaluation follows the arrows.

A neuron fits the same mould. Each input meets its weight at a multiplication node, the products flow into an addition node, the bias joins at another addition, and the result passes through a ReLU node. A whole network is this pattern repeated, and even a language model with billions of parameters is, underneath, one enormous graph made of the same few kinds of node.

The key design decision is that every value remembers where it came from. When we compute a times b, the result does not just store the number minus six; it also stores a link to a and to b, and a note that the operation was multiplication. That memory costs a little storage, but it is precisely what will let us walk the graph backwards later and ask how each input influenced the output.

In code, we can build this with a small class called Value. It wraps a number, keeps the set of values that produced it, and records the name of the operation, and by defining Python's addition and multiplication for it, ordinary expressions like a times b plus c build the graph automatically as they run. This is the first piece of your own tiny automatic differentiation engine, and you will write it in this lesson's problems.

PyTorch works in the same way. Every time a model runs its forward pass, the library quietly records a node for each operation it performs, building the graph as the code runs, and that record is what makes a single call to backward possible.

So the forward pass computes the answer and, as a side effect, leaves behind a map of how it got there. In the next lesson we walk along that map in reverse, and that reverse journey is backpropagation.
